extra.message: Insecure Deserialization via pickle.loads() in /ops/bundle — Remote code execution on the server via crafted pickle payload. [verified: Same as finding 4: attacker-controlled bytes are deserialized via `pickle.loads(raw)` at line ~61. `_wrk_gate` checks a header token but performs zero payload validation.]

Insecure Deserialization via pickle.loads() in /ops/bundle — Remote code execution upon deserialization, enabling full server compromise including arbitrary command execution, data theft, and malware installation. [verified: Attacker-controlled raw bytes (from request body or `blob` query param, optionally base64-decoded) are deserialized via `pickle.loads(raw)` at line ~76. Pickle on untrusted data allows arbitrary code execution; `_wrk_gate` does not validate the payload.]

Python Code Injection via eval() in /ops/formula — Arbitrary Python code execution on the server, leading to data exfiltration, system compromise, or lateral movement. [verified: Same as finding 1: user-controlled `expr` flows directly to `eval(expr, {"__builtins__": {}}, ...)` at line ~77. Empty `__builtins__` is a bypassable sandbox; `_wrk_gate` provides no input sanitization.]

Python Code Injection via eval() in /ops/formula — Arbitrary Python code execution on the server, enabling full system compromise including data exfiltration, credential theft, and lateral movement. [verified: User-controlled `expr` query parameter is passed directly to `eval(expr, {"__builtins__": {}}, ...)` at line ~96. Clearing `__builtins__` is a known-bypassable sandbox; the `_wrk_gate` auth check does not neutralize the code-injection sink.]

Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) via Jinja2 in /ops/jinja — Remote code execution, arbitrary file read, and sensitive data exposure through Jinja2 template expression injection. [verified: Same as finding 2: user-controlled `fragment` is injected into `Template("Result: " + fragment).render()` at line ~117. `_wrk_gate` authenticates but does not prevent SSTI.]

Server-Side Template Injection via Jinja2 in /ops/jinja — Remote code execution via SSTI, enabling an attacker to read server-side configuration, environment variables, and potentially achieve full system compromise. [verified: User-controlled `fragment` query parameter is concatenated into a Jinja2 template string `Template("Result: " + fragment).render()` at line ~130, enabling SSTI. `_wrk_gate` authenticates but does not sanitize the template input.]

OS Command Injection via /ops/shell ping endpoint — Remote code execution on the application server with the privileges of the server process — full system compromise. [verified: Same as finding 0: user-controlled `host` is concatenated unsanitized into `os.system("ping -c 1 " + host)` at line ~146. `_wrk_gate` authenticates but does not validate shell input.]

Path Traversal / Arbitrary File Write in /ops/vault — Arbitrary file write on the server filesystem — could overwrite application code, configuration, SSH keys, or write to startup scripts for persistence. [verified: Same as finding 8: user-controlled `ref` is used unsanitized in `BASE_EXPORT_DIR / f"{ref}.json"` at line ~67, enabling path traversal with auto-created parent directories. `_wrk_gate` provides no path validation.]

Path Traversal / Arbitrary File Write in /ops/vault — An attacker can write arbitrary JSON content to any location on the filesystem accessible to the process, potentially overwriting configuration files, planting webshells, or corrupting application data. [verified: User-controlled `ref` parameter is interpolated into `BASE_EXPORT_DIR / f"{ref}.json"` at line ~90 with no path sanitization, allowing `../` traversal. `target.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` facilitates writes to arbitrary locations. `_wrk_gate` provides no path validation.]

Path Traversal / Arbitrary File Write in /ops/dock — Arbitrary file write of attacker-controlled bytes to any writable path, enabling code execution, configuration modification, or persistence. [verified: Same as finding 9: user-controlled `name` is used directly in `BASE_EXPORT_DIR / name` at line ~123 with no sanitization; body bytes are written to the traversed path. `_wrk_gate` provides no path validation.]

NoSQL Injection via raw MongoDB query in /ops/mongo — Arbitrary MongoDB data access, authentication bypass, data exfiltration, or denial of service. [verified: Same as finding 6: user-controlled JSON filter is passed raw to `find_one(query)` at line ~133. `_wrk_gate` provides no query sanitization.]

Path Traversal / Arbitrary File Write in /ops/dock — An attacker can write arbitrary binary content to any location on the filesystem, potentially overwriting application files, planting malware, or achieving code execution. [verified: User-controlled `name` query parameter is used directly in `BASE_EXPORT_DIR / name` at line ~135 with no path sanitization; arbitrary request-body bytes are written via `write_bytes`. `_wrk_gate` provides no path validation.]

XML External Entity (XXE) Injection in /ops/xml — Arbitrary local file read, internal network scanning via SSRF, and denial of service through XML entity expansion. [verified: Same as finding 5: attacker-supplied XML is parsed with DTD/entity resolution enabled at line ~139. `_wrk_gate` auth does not sanitize the XML payload.]

Missing rate limiting on login endpoint enables brute-force password attacks — An attacker can brute-force user passwords by sending unlimited login attempts without triggering any lockout, delay, or alert. Combined with user enumeration via the register endpoint, targeted credential stuffing becomes practical. [verified: Identical to finding 1 — zero rate limiting exists on any authentication endpoint; grep across the entire codebase for rate.limit/throttl/brute.force/slowapi/attempt/lockout/captcha returned no matches, and no rate-limiting package is in requirements.txt, leaving login open to unlimited brute-force.]

Session Cookie Missing Secure Flag on Registration — In a production HTTPS deployment, the session cookie set after registration can be transmitted over unencrypted connections, enabling network attackers to steal the session and impersonate the user. [verified: The register endpoint at line 493 hardcodes secure=False when setting the session cookie, while the login endpoint reads COOKIE_SECURE from the environment; in a production HTTPS deployment where COOKIE_SECURE=true, the registration cookie would still lack the Secure flag, exposing the session token to network interception.]

Session Cookie Missing Secure Flag in Registration — Session hijacking via network sniffing on unencrypted connections — an attacker can steal session cookies and impersonate users. [verified: Identical to finding 2 — register at line 493 hardcodes secure=False ignoring the COOKIE_SECURE env var that the login endpoint respects; in production HTTPS deployments the session cookie after registration lacks the Secure flag.]

Password Reset Token Exposed in Logs and API Response — Account takeover — an attacker with access to the log file or dev API response can reset any user's password. [verified: When APP_ENV != 'production' (default 'local' per .env.example), the raw password reset token is returned directly in the API response body as dev_reset_token (line ~515), enabling immediate account takeover by requesting a reset and reading the token from the response — no authentication required.]

Sensitive Authorization Header and Request Body in Application Logs — Real credentials/API keys sent in the Authorization header are captured in plaintext logs, enabling credential theft from log files. Log injection via body content allows forged log entries. [verified: The handler unconditionally logs request.headers.get("authorization") via logger.warning with no redaction; anyone possessing the INTERNAL_OPS_TOKEN can force real credentials into application logs, and raw body bytes decoded into the log format string enable newline-based log injection.]

Open Redirect in /ops/after — Phishing attacks — redirecting authenticated users to attacker-controlled sites to steal credentials or session tokens. [verified: Same as finding 7: user-controlled `lane` is passed directly to `RedirectResponse(lane)` at line ~39 with no URL validation. `_wrk_gate` authenticates but does not restrict redirect targets.]

Reflected XSS via Jinja2 |safe filter in /ops/blurb — Cross-site scripting — an attacker can inject arbitrary JavaScript that executes in the victim's browser context, enabling session theft, credential phishing, or DOM manipulation. [verified: Same as finding 3: user-controlled `card` is rendered with `|safe` at line ~87, disabling auto-escaping and returning `HTMLResponse`. `_wrk_gate` provides no output sanitization.]

Denial of Service via Unbounded Memory Allocation in /ops/spool — An attacker can cause the application server to exhaust memory and crash, denying service to legitimate users. [verified: User-controlled `count` query parameter feeds `range(count)` at line ~101 with no upper bound, allowing memory-exhaustion DoS. `_wrk_gate` auth does not limit the input magnitude.]

Cross-Site Scripting via Jinja2 |safe filter in /ops/blurb — An attacker can execute arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser context, enabling session theft, credential phishing, and execution of operations using the victim's privileges. [verified: User-controlled `card` query parameter is rendered via `Template("{{ card|safe }}").render(card=card)` with the `|safe` filter disabling auto-escaping at line ~107; response is `HTMLResponse`. `_wrk_gate` provides auth but no output sanitization.]

Missing Security Headers on Application Responses — Users are vulnerable to clickjacking attacks, MIME-type sniffing exploits, and man-in-the-middle downgrade attacks due to absent HSTS, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, and CSP headers. [verified: No security headers (HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, CSP) are set anywhere—only CORSMiddleware is added (line 74); the app serves HTML via frontend static files (line 1261) making clickjacking and MIME-sniffing relevant with no compensating control.]

Login CSRF - Missing CSRF Protection on Login Endpoint — Attacker can force victim to log into attacker-controlled account; victim may then unknowingly upload sensitive proof documents, create jobs with PII, or send messages visible to the attacker. [verified: Login endpoint (line 416) lacks the require_csrf dependency present on 24 other state-changing endpoints; an attacker can craft a cross-origin form POST that sets the attacker's session cookie in the victim's browser, and SameSite=Lax does not block Set-Cookie processing from cross-origin responses.]

Missing Rate Limiting on Registration Endpoint — Attacker can create unlimited accounts causing database bloat, resource exhaustion, and spam customer records. [verified: No rate limiting middleware, dependency, or anti-automation exists anywhere in the codebase (confirmed by full search); the register endpoint creates four database records per call with no throttling, enabling resource exhaustion and database bloat.]

Account Enumeration via Registration Response — An attacker can compile a list of valid user accounts, enabling targeted credential-stuffing, phishing campaigns, or social-engineering attacks against known users of the platform. [verified: The /api/auth/register endpoint is public (no auth dependency) and returns distinct 409 'An account with this email already exists' when a duplicate email is detected (line 456), while other error conditions produce different responses — no middleware or control masks this distinction, allowing unauthenticated enumeration of registered emails.]

User Enumeration via Registration Response — An attacker can enumerate valid user email addresses in the system for targeted attacks, credential stuffing, or social engineering. [verified: Identical to finding 0 — the public /api/auth/register endpoint returns HTTP 409 with a distinct message when the email already exists (line 456), enabling unauthenticated email enumeration with no compensating control.]

Missing Rate Limiting on Password Reset Request Endpoint — Attacker can flood specific user email addresses with repeated password reset requests causing log file growth, database churn, and user harassment. [verified: No rate limiting exists application-wide; each request to /api/auth/password-reset/request performs a file write and database commit with no throttling, allowing log file growth, database churn, and user harassment.]

CSV Formula Injection in Data Exports — When an administrator or dispatcher opens the exported CSV in a spreadsheet application, injected formulas can execute commands on their machine (Windows) or exfiltrate spreadsheet data to attacker-controlled servers, enabling client-side code execution and data theft. [verified: CSV export functions (export_incidents at line ~1478, export_completions at ~1446, export_routes at ~1407) write user-controlled fields (customer_summary, internal_notes, resolution, billing_ref) directly via csv.DictWriter.writerow() with zero sanitization of formula-trigger characters (=, +, -, @); an authenticated user who creates incidents or jobs can inject formula payloads that execute when ]

Password Reset Token Leaked to Browser in Non-Production Mode — Account takeover via intercepted reset token when APP_ENV is misconfigured; the raw token grants password-reset capability for 30 minutes. [verified: The password-reset endpoint (public, line 498) returns the raw reset token in JSON when APP_ENV != 'production' (line 513), and .env.example defaults APP_ENV=local (line 3). An attacker can trigger a reset for any registered email and receive the raw token in the browser DOM (line 172), enabling account takeover within the 30-minute window.]

CORS Origin Reflection with Credentials in /ops/origin — Cross-origin attacks with credentials — a malicious site can make authenticated requests to the API on behalf of the victim. [verified: Same as finding 10: the endpoint reflects `Origin` into CORS headers with credentials at line ~101. The `x-internal-token` requirement prevents browser-based cross-origin exploitation, but the misconfiguration is genuinely present on a reachable path.]

CORS Origin Reflection with Credentials in /ops/origin — Any website can make authenticated cross-origin requests to the API on behalf of a logged-in user, enabling data theft and state-changing operations from the victim's session. [verified: The `/ops/origin` endpoint reflects the request `Origin` header into `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` and sets `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` at line ~118. The endpoint requires `x-internal-token`, which browser cross-origin requests cannot include, limiting practical exploitability.]

Sensitive Password Reset Tokens Logged to Plaintext File — An attacker with read access to the local_mocks/password_resets.log file (via any file-read vulnerability or misconfiguration) can obtain valid password reset tokens and take over arbitrary user accounts. [verified: Raw password reset tokens are unconditionally written to local_mocks/password_resets.log (line 473) in all environments including production; exploitation requires filesystem read access or a separate path-traversal vulnerability since this directory is not served as static files, but the sensitive credential is genuinely stored in plaintext.]

Missing Rate Limiting on Password Reset Confirmation Endpoint — Unlimited password reset confirmation attempts, enabling resource consumption and reducing defense-in-depth against token guessing. [verified: No rate limiting exists, but the reset token uses secrets.token_urlsafe(36) (288 bits of entropy) making brute-force infeasible; the missing control is a genuine defense-in-depth gap with only resource-consumption impact per attempt.]
